AddChannelMemberRequest.description:
Add one person to a channel, by id.

Singular, not "add member(s)": a batch add has no honest status code when
three of five ids are already in the channel. Five calls do.

By id and never by email, because Messaging owns no user records and must
not read Auth's tables (Conventions §2) — it cannot resolve an address, and
it does not check that the id names a real user either. The browser holds a
token entitling it to both services and does the resolving.
AddChannelMemberRequest.title: AddChannelMemberRequest

Attachment.description:
A file on a message: what the Asset service said when it was claimed.

**No URL.** A URL is short-lived and per-viewer, so it is minted on demand
by `GET /messages/{id}/attachments/{assetId}/download-url`, which checks the
caller can see the message. This is only enough to draw a chip.
Attachment.title: Attachment

AttachmentDownloadResponse.description: A short-lived URL to GET one attachment's bytes from object storage.
AttachmentDownloadResponse.title: AttachmentDownloadResponse

ChannelMemberResponse.description:
One membership row. A bare `userId`: there is no name here to give.

The SPA renders the name by looking the id up in Auth's workspace member
list, which it is already entitled to read.
ChannelMemberResponse.title: ChannelMemberResponse

ChannelResponse.description:
A channel as the API reports it.

No `workspaceId`: a channel is always in the workspace named by the caller's
`wsp` claim, and echoing it back invites a client to start sending it.

`version` and `myRole` are unused by the create-and-list surface. They ship
now because the alternative is changing this shape again one slice later —
`version` is what an edit sends back for optimistic concurrency, and
`myRole` is what decides whether the UI offers the admin controls.

`lastReadId` and `unreadCount` are required and have no default, on purpose:
a default drops a field from the OpenAPI `required` list, and the generated
TypeScript would make every sidebar render null-check a count the server
always sends. A channel just created reports `null` and `0`.
ChannelResponse.title: ChannelResponse

CreateChannelRequest.description:
Create a channel in the caller's workspace.

`name` is checked in the domain rather than by a Pydantic pattern, so every
broken rule gets its own message in the `errors` map instead of one opaque
"string does not match regex". Only the outer bound is here, to keep an
unbounded body from reaching the domain at all.
CreateChannelRequest.title: CreateChannelRequest

EditMessageRequest.description:
Rewrite a message.

**Not a JSON Merge Patch of `Message`.** Conventions §4 defines `PATCH` that
way, and under RFC 7386 `{"version": 3}` would mean *assign 3 to version* —
the exact opposite of what it means here. `version` is a precondition: the
version the caller last saw, which the server checks and refuses on.

Both fields are required. There is exactly one editable field on a message,
so "absent means leave it alone" has nothing to express — the
`model_fields_set` idiom `UpdateChannelRequest` needs is deliberately not
used here, rather than forgotten.

`max_length` is `MAX_BODY_FIELD_LENGTH`, the same bound `SendMessageRequest`
carries — one constant, not two numbers to drift apart.
EditMessageRequest.title: EditMessageRequest

MarkReadRequest.description:
Mark a channel read up to and including one message.

The message must be in the channel named by the path. Marking an older
message than the one already marked is accepted and changes nothing — two
tabs racing each other is the normal case, not a conflict.
MarkReadRequest.title: MarkReadRequest

MessageListResponse.description: The list envelope from Conventions §4.1. Newest first.
MessageListResponse.title: MessageListResponse

MessageResponse.description:
A message as the API reports it (spec §3.1.3).

One absence and two presences are all deliberate.

`replyCount` and `lastReplyAt` summarise a root's live (not deleted) replies
and are `0` and `null` on everything else — a reply, a message nobody
answered, a freshly sent one. Both are required with no default, for the
reason `ChannelResponse` gives: a default drops them from OpenAPI `required`.
A deleted root keeps its summary (R10).

`reactions` is a summary — one entry per emoji anyone used, with the count
and whether the caller is one of them — and it is `[]` rather than absent
when nobody has reacted. `attachments` is `[]` when there are none, in the
order the sender attached them, and **always `[]` on a deleted message**:
the tombstone shows no files.

No `workspaceId`, for the reason `ChannelResponse` gives: it is the token's
`wsp` claim, and echoing it invites a client to start sending it.

`authorId` is a bare id and there is no user expansion. Messaging owns no
user records and must not read Auth's tables (Conventions §2); the browser
resolves the name from Auth's own workspace directory, holding a token that
already entitles it to both.

**`body` is `""` on a deleted message, never `null` and never the original
text.** The redaction is server-side and the type stays non-null, so the
generated TypeScript does not force a null check at every render site. The
client renders "this message was deleted" from `deletedAt`, not from an
empty body.
MessageResponse.title: MessageResponse

ReactionRequest.description:
React with one emoji.

The shortcode only — the message is in the path and the person is the
token's `sub`. Validated against the server's allowlist in the domain rather
than by a Pydantic `Literal`, so a rejected value gets a message under
`errors.emoji` like every other broken rule instead of an opaque enum error
from the wrong layer. `max_length` is the column width, an outer bound and
not the rule.
ReactionRequest.title: ReactionRequest

ReactionSummary.description:
One emoji on a message: how many people, and whether you are one of them.

**Counts, never user ids.** A "who reacted" list is a second feature with a
privacy question of its own, and shipping the ids to every client now would
decide it silently.

`reacted` is computed for the caller on every request, which is also why it
can never be broadcast: a room emit delivers one payload to everyone, so
every recipient would receive whoever acted last. `reaction_changed` carries
the actor's id instead, and each client decides its own lit state.
ReactionSummary.title: ReactionSummary

SendMessageRequest.description:
Say something in a channel, or reply to a message in it, optionally with files.

No `channelId` — it is in the path; no `authorId` — it is the token's `sub`.
`threadRootId` names the message being replied to: a reply to a reply is
filed under the root, and a root that is unknown or in another channel is a
404.

`attachmentIds` are assets the caller has uploaded and confirmed, in the
order they should appear. How many, and whether any is listed twice, are
rules checked in the domain so the answer can say which — not a Pydantic
bound from the wrong layer. The body may be empty only when there is at least
one.

`max_length` on the body is a static outer bound and **not** the rule — see
`MAX_BODY_FIELD_LENGTH`.
SendMessageRequest.title: SendMessageRequest

ThreadResponse.description:
A thread: its root, and a cursor page of its replies, newest first.

The root travels with every page because the panel needs it even when it is
not in loaded history (an old root, or one opened from the URL), and one
request is one loading state. Replies include tombstones (R5).
ThreadResponse.title: ThreadResponse

UpdateChannelRequest.description:
Rename a channel, or change its topic.

`version` is required and is the version the client last read. The expected
version travels in the body rather than in an `If-Match` header: nothing on
this platform emits or parses an ETag, and the `Channel` DTO already carries
the number the SPA holds in its cache.

There is no `archivedAt`. Archiving is `DELETE /channels/{id}`, so no client
ever writes a server clock into a timestamp column.

An absent `topic` leaves the topic alone; an explicit `null` clears it. The
router tells them apart with `model_fields_set`, which is why the two cases
do not need two fields.
UpdateChannelRequest.title: UpdateChannelRequest

get.description:
Channels in the caller's workspace that the caller may know about.

Public channels regardless of membership, plus anything else they have
joined; archived channels are excluded. Alphabetical, cursor-paginated
(Conventions §4.1) — never `OFFSET`.

post.description: Create a channel, with the caller as its admin.

delete.description:
Archive a channel — the soft delete from spec §4. Channel admins only.

Unconditional and one-way. Every read in this service goes through
`get_visible`, which filters `archived_at IS NULL`, so an archived channel
and its messages are unreachable afterwards by anyone including the admin
who archived it. Archiving a second time is therefore a 404, which is
consistent rather than a case to special-case into a 204.

The archived channel is returned, since it is the last chance anyone gets to
see it and the SPA needs the row it is navigating away from. It is re-read
with `refresh` rather than through `get_visible`, which by now filters it
out — that being the whole point of the write.

get.description: One channel, if the caller may know it exists — with their read state.

patch.description:
Rename a channel, or change its topic. Channel admins only.

The response is re-read through `get_visible` rather than built from the
object in the session: the update went through Core, so the in-session row
is stale and would report the old name back to the client that just changed
it. What comes back is what was stored.

get.description:
Who is in a channel the caller can see.

Guarded by visibility, not by membership — spec §3.1 says "channel member",
and taken literally that would let Grace see `#general` in her sidebar, read
every word in it, and get a 403 for asking who else is there. A private
channel is invisible to non-members already, so the only case this widens is
a public one, where the membership is not a secret from a workspace that can
already read the conversation.

Ordered by user id, which is arbitrary to a human on purpose: Messaging
holds no display names, so it has no meaningful order to offer. The panel
sorts the page it receives.

post.description:
Add someone to a channel. Channel admins only, including adding yourself.

There is no self-join in this scope: joining a channel is something an admin
does to you, not something you do.

delete.description:
Remove someone from a channel. Channel admins only.

Nothing else is revoked: channel membership is in no token, so unlike Auth's
workspace removal there are no sessions to end here. A reviewer who
remembers that route will look for the equivalent — there is none to write.

get.description:
A channel's history, newest first, cursor-paginated (Conventions §4.1).

Deleted messages are included, with their bodies redacted — the tombstone is
part of the history, not something the client reconstructs.

post.description:
Say something in a channel the caller can see, with up to ten files.

Spec §3.1 keeps this as the REST fallback once the Socket.IO send exists;
both call the same domain function, so the rules cannot drift between them.

**Claim, then insert.** Everything that can be refused is refused first —
visibility, the attachment count, the body — then the message's id is
chosen, its assets are claimed from Asset for that id, and only then is the
message written. A refused or unreachable claim (409, 503) leaves nothing
behind. The body is checked *before* the claim: a bad body must not claim
assets for a message that will never exist.

Mark a channel read up to and including one message.

**204 either way** — whether the marker moved or was already further on.
The client sent the newest message it has shown, and "you had already read
that" is not an error it could act on.

The receipt goes to the caller's *other* sessions only, and only when the
marker moved. Nobody else is told how far anyone has read.

delete.description:
Tombstone a message. The author, or an admin of its channel.

**200 with the tombstoned message, not 204.** A delete here does not remove
a row from the list — it stays with `body: ""` and `deletedAt` set, and the
client has to render it. With 204 the client would have to refetch a page it
is already holding to learn what to draw; with the row in hand it replaces
one entry in its cache. The same argument as returning the created row from
a `POST`, and a deliberate deviation from "DELETE returns 204" rather than a
surprise in the OpenAPI document.

Deleting twice returns the same tombstone, unchanged — and enqueues no
second index job, because nothing about the document changed.

get.description: One message, if the caller can see the channel it is in.

patch.description:
Rewrite a message. **The author, and nobody else.**

Not even a channel admin, who *can* delete this message. That asymmetry is
the point rather than an oversight: deleting someone's words is moderation,
and rewriting them under their name is forgery.

403 here and not 404, which is the opposite of the channel rules two files
over — and correct. A message the caller cannot see never reaches this
check; one they can see is already on their screen, so refusing the edit
discloses nothing, and a 404 would be a lie about a row they are looking at.

There is no time window (register D8d).

get.description:
A short-lived URL for one attachment, for anyone who can see the message.

**This is where download authorization lives** (register D43): Asset has no
public download route, so a file can only be fetched through a message, and a
message can only be seen by someone who can see its channel.

A channel the caller cannot see, or no such message, is the usual `No such
channel.`. After that Messaging's *own* record decides: a deleted message, or
an asset that is not on this one, is `No such attachment.` without asking
Asset, which would happily mint a URL for either. 503 when Asset is down.

post.description:
React to a message. Reacting again with the same emoji changes nothing.

**200 rather than 201.** The useful answer is the message's new counts, and
a repeat is not a creation — there is no new resource to point at either
time, because a reaction is not addressable on its own.

delete.description:
Take a reaction back.

**No tombstone check, unlike the add.** Deleting a message clears its
reactions, so there is never anything on one to remove — and a second tab
that has already removed it must not be told the message is in the wrong
state for what is a no-op.

get.description:
A root and a page of its replies, newest first, tombstones included.

Visibility is the guard, as on every message route (spec §3.1.1). Naming a
reply is a 404 with its own wording: the caller can see the reply, so
saying what is wrong with the id leaks nothing.

Messages matching every word of `q`, newest first, in channels the caller can see.

**A short page is not the last page** — hydration can drop a hit whose row
was deleted after it was indexed. Only `nextCursor: null` means the end.
